It is important to notice that while the proof of Birkhoff’s theorem tells us abstractly how to construct relatively free lattices, it does not tell us how to solve the word problem for them. Consider the variety \(\mathbf M\) of modular lattices. Richard Dedekind [6] showed in the 1890’s that \(F_{\mathbf M}(3)\) has 28 elements; it is drawn in Figure 9.2. On the other hand, Ralph Freese [9] proved in 1980 that the word problem for \(F_{\mathbf M}(5)\) is unsolvable: there is no algorithm for determining whether \(p=q\) in \(F_{\mathbf M}(5)\). Christian Herrmann [10] later showed that the word problem for \(F_{\mathbf M}(4)\) is also unsolvable. It follows, by the way, that the variety of modular lattices is not generated by its finite members:² there is a lattice equation which holds in all finite modular lattices, but not in all modular lattices.
